title: Scalar Variables - Numbers & Evaluate
description: Calculate the ship's total power output from three reactors. You'll need to store numeric values, add them together, find the average, and determine if there's a power deficit.

story.setup: The ship's power systems need calibration. MENTOR-9 pulls up a diagnostic readout.
story.context: PROTO-7, we need to calculate total power output. We have three reactors, each producing different amounts. We can't just log numbers—we need to DO MATH on them. That's where the Evaluate keyword comes in.
story.success: Excellent! You've performed calculations with Evaluate. Addition, subtraction, multiplication, division—all the basic operations. This is how robots think numerically!

instructions: Store three reactor power values: '150', '200', and '175' in variables '${reactor_1}', '${reactor_2}', '${reactor_3}'
Calculate the total power from all three reactors and store in '${total_power}'
Calculate the average power output and store in '${average_power}'
Calculate the power deficit (required: 600, actual: total) and store in '${deficit}'
Log the total power with message: 'Total power: ${total_power}'
Log the average power with message: 'Average power: ${average_power}'
Log the deficit with message: 'Power deficit: ${deficit}'
Run the code and verify your calculations in the Console tab
hints: You can use variables in expressions: ${var1} + ${var2}

theory.title: Scalar Variables: Numbers & Math with Evaluate
theory.content:
MENTOR-9 gestures to the ship's power distribution panel, numbers flickering across holographic displays.

Look at this. Three reactors, different outputs. We can't manually calculate the total every time. We need the computer to do the math. That's what Evaluate does—it performs calculations.

Numbers: Integers and Floats

Remember how Robot Framework treats everything as strings by default? When you need actual numbers for math, wrap them in ${}:

*** Variables ***
${STRING}            This is a string
${STILL_STRING}      8270    # Text: characters 8, 2, 7, 0
${INTEGER}           ${42}   # Integer (whole number)
${FLOAT}             ${3.14} # Float (decimal number)

The difference: 42 is text, ${42} is a number. But storing numbers isn't enough—we need to calculate with them.

The Evaluate Keyword

Evaluate executes Python math expressions. It's your calculator:

${result}    Evaluate    10 + 5    # Returns 15

All the math operators work: + (add), - (subtract), * (multiply), / (divide), // (integer divide), % (remainder), ** (power).

Standard math rules apply: multiplication/division happen before addition/subtraction. Use parentheses to change order.

Using Variables in Calculations

Use variables in expressions—Robot Framework substitutes their values:

*** Test Cases ***
Area Calculation
    ${width}     10
    ${height}    5
    ${area}      Evaluate    ${width} * ${height}
    Log    Area: ${area}

Note: Numbers auto-convert to strings when logging.
